claims.source: As the branching pathway declines in enzymatic efficiency going from MGAT1 to MGAT5, Mgat2 deficiency also impacts a much greater percentage of cell surface glycans than Mgat5 deletion (Wang et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and knowledge of enzyme kinetics in the pathway.

claims.claim: Examination of peripheral T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice indicated loss of Mgat2 in most but not all T cells as assayed by flow cytometry with L-PHA.
claims.source: Examination of peripheral T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice indicated loss of Mgat2 in most but not all T cells as assayed by flow cytometry with the plant lectin L-PHA (Phaseolus vulgaris, leukoagglutinin) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: β1,6GlcNAc-branched N-glycans produced by MGAT5 specifically bind L-PHA.
claims.source: β1,6GlcNAc-branched N-glycans produced by MGAT5 specifically bind L-PHA, structures that are also lost following Mgat2 deletion (Demetriou et al., 2001; Cummings and Kornfeld, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a similar degree of activation and proliferation in response to anti-CD3 despite the more dramatic reduction in LacNAc branching in Mgat2 deficient T cells.
claims.source: Surprisingly, Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a similar degree of activation and proliferation in response to anti-CD3 (an antibody which induces TCR clustering and signaling) despite the more dramatic reduction in LacNAc branching in Mgat2 deficient T cells (Figure 1A,B,D and E).
claims.evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Mgat5 deletion resulted in a significant reduction in the ability of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells to bind galectin-3.
claims.source: Mgat5 deletion resulted in a significant reduction in the ability of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells to bind galectin-3 (Figure 1C and F), consistent with previously published results (Demetriou et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in the referenced figures and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Mgat2 deficiency produced no additional decrease in galectin-3 binding compared to Mgat5 deficiency.
claims.source: However, Mgat2 deficiency produced no additional decrease in galectin-3 binding (Figure 1C and F), suggesting comparable LacNAc content at the cell surface despite a marked reduction in LacNAc branches in Mgat2 relative to Mgat5 deficient T cells.
claims.evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Compensatory maintenance of cell surface LacNAc content in Mgat2 deficient T cells would primarily occur by poly-LacNAc extension of the MGAT1 generated branch.
claims.source: Since the branching pathway enzymes act sequentially, we hypothesized that compensatory maintenance of cell surface LacNAc content in Mgat2 deficient T cells would primarily occur by poly-LacNAc extension of the MGAT1 generated branch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on knowledge of the pathway that is then tested experimentally.

claims.claim: LEA binds to poly-LacNAc structures containing at least three repeating LacNAc units.
claims.source: LEA binds to poly-LacNAc structures containing at least three repeating LacNAc units (Kawashima et al., 1990; Merkle and Cummings, 1987).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Wild type and Mgat5-/- T cells and thymocytes expressed very low levels of poly-LacNAc.
claims.source: Wild type and Mgat5-/- T cells and thymocytes expressed very low levels of poly-LacNAc.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LEA staining data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: In Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice, loss of L-PHA staining was accompanied by a ~100 fold increase in LEA staining.
claims.source: However, in Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice, loss of L-PHA staining was accompanied by a ~100 fold increase in LEA staining.
claims.evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The loss of L-PHA binding and the increase in LEA binding appeared to occur concurrently during the double positive stage of thymocyte development, shortly after the Lck promoter driven Cre is first expressed, and were maintained through the single positive stage and in peripheral T cells.
claims.source: The loss of L-PHA binding and the increase in LEA binding appeared to occur concurrently during the double positive stage of thymocyte development, shortly after the Lck promoter driven Cre is first expressed, and were maintained through the single positive stage and in peripheral T cells (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by developmental analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Treatment of various cell types with swainsonine indicated that homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc was a general feature of many cell types including epithelial, mesenchymal, and hematopoietic cells; with the greatest responses in the latter.
claims.source: Treatment of various cell types with swainsonine (SW), a mannosidase II inhibitor which blocks N-glycan processing between MGAT1 and MGAT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicated that homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc was a general feature of many cell types including epithelial, mesenchymal, and hematopoietic cells; with the greatest responses in the latter (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1H showing LEA induction across multiple cell types.

claims.claim: Poly-LacNAc may occur on N-glycans as well as O-glycans and glycolipids.
claims.source: Poly-LacNAc may occur on N-glycans as well as O-glycans and glycolipids (Fukuda et al., 1986; Watanabe et al., 1979).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: LEA has been reported to bind to high-mannose structures in addition to poly-LacNAc.
claims.source: Furthermore, LEA has been reported to bind to high-mannose structures in addition to poly-LacNAc (Oguri, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: PNGase F treatment of live cells incompletely removes N-glycans, with a four hour treatment of Mgat2f/f T cells reducing cell surface L-PHA binding by ~50%.
claims.source: PNGase F treatment of live cells incompletely removes N-glycans, with a four hour treatment of Mgat2f/f T cells reducing cell surface L-PHA binding by ~50% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claims.claim: PNGase F treatment resulted in a >80% reduction in LEA binding in Mgat2 deficient T cells, suggesting that the vast majority of LEA staining was due to cell surface N-glycans.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the same treatment resulted in a >80% reduction in LEA binding in Mgat2 deficient T cells, suggesting that the vast majority of LEA staining was due to cell surface N-glycans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claims.claim: Mgat1 deficiency blocks all branching and poly-LacNAc extension in N-glycans, but not O-glycans or glycolipids.
claims.source: Mgat1 deficiency blocks all branching and poly-LacNAc extension in N-glycans, but not O-glycans or glycolipids.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of the biosynthetic pathway.

claims.claim: Unlike Mgat2 deficiency, Mgat1 deficient thymocytes do not show an increase in LEA staining concurrent with the loss in L-PHA staining.
claims.source: Indeed, unlike Mgat2 deficiency, Mgat1 deficient thymocytes do not show an increase in LEA staining concurrent with the loss in L-PHA staining (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: SW increases LEA staining in CHO cells but not Mgat1 deficient CHO (Lec1) cells.
claims.source: Similarly, SW increases LEA staining in CHO cells but not Mgat1 deficient CHO (Lec1) cells (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2B and C.

claims.claim: Increased LEA staining induced by SW treatment of T cells was reversed by the mannosidase I inhibitors deoxymannojirimycin (DMN) and kifunensine (kif), which block the N-glycan pathway prior to MGAT1.
claims.source: Furthermore, increased LEA staining induced by SW treatment of T cells was reversed by the mannosidase I inhibitors deoxymannojirimycin (DMN) and kifunensine (kif), which block the N-glycan pathway prior to MGAT1 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: MALDI-TOF-MS of N-glycans derived from SW treated Jurkat T cells confirmed the presence of hybrid N-glycans with up to two poly-LacNAc extended branches.
claims.source: MALDI-TOF-MS of N-glycans derived from SW treated Jurkat T cells confirmed the presence of hybrid N-glycans with up to two poly-LacNAc extended branches (m/z 2897, 3102, 3347, 3551, and 4000 in Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Endo-β-galactosidase digestion confirmed the presence of longer poly-LacNAc chains after SW treatment.
claims.source: The non-treated cells had a ratio of 0.5, which increased to 1.1 in the SW treated cells (Figure 2F and G), confirming the presence of longer poly-LacNAc chains after SW treatment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data after enzymatic digestion shown in Figures 2F and G.

claims.claim: SW treatment alone moderately reduced galectin-3 binding, but the addition of kifunensine dramatically reduced galectin-3 binding of Jurkat T cells.
claims.source: Whereas SW treatment alone moderately reduced galectin-3 binding, the addition of kifunensine dramatically reduced galectin-3 binding of Jurkat T cells (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: SW treatment alone caused significant increases in both anti-CD3 induced activation and proliferation of primary human T cells.
claims.source: As previously shown, SW treatment alone caused significant increases in both anti-CD3 induced activation and proliferation of primary human T cells (Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The addition of kifunensine or DMN to SW treatment resulted in much greater T cell hyperactivity, particularly at lower doses of anti-CD3.
claims.source: However, the addition of kifunensine or DMN resulted in much greater hyperactivity, particularly at lower doses of anti-CD3.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3B and C.

claims.claim: Careful titration of kifunensine in the presence of SW caused a dose dependent decrease in LEA binding and increase in CD69 induction, indicating that poly-LacNAc extension dose dependently regulates T cell activation thresholds.
claims.source: Careful titration of kifunensine in the presence of SW did not further reduce L-PHA binding, yet caused a dose dependent decrease in LEA binding and increase in CD69 induction, indicating that poly-LacNAc extension dose dependently regulates T cell activation thresholds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in the referenced figure supplement.

claims.claim: T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+::B3gnt2-/- mice showed significantly reduced galectin-3 binding when compared to Mgat2 deficient T cells, confirming reduced LacNAc content.
claims.source: Indeed, T cells from Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+::B3gnt2-/- mice showed significantly reduced galectin-3 binding when compared to Mgat2 deficient T cells, confirming reduced LacNAc content (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of homeostatic poly-LacNAc extension resulted in significantly increased T cell hyperactivity.
claims.source: Directly comparing T cell activation between these lines showed that both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of homeostatic poly-LacNAc extension resulted in significantly increased T cell hyperactivity (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Vehicle treated Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice displayed a significantly more severe EAE than vehicle treated Mgat2f/f mice.
claims.source: As expected, vehicle treated Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice displayed a significantly more severe EAE than vehicle treated Mgat2f/f mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by EAE clinical score data in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Kifunensine treatment of Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice resulted in a dramatic increase in clinical score and disease incidence early in the disease course.
claims.source: However, kifunensine treatment of Mgat2f/f::Lck-Cre+ mice resulted in a dramatic increase in clinical score and disease incidence early in the disease course, a difference that narrowed later in the absence of kifunensine (Figure 3F and Figure 3—supplement figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EAE data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Kifunensine treated mice had more pro-inflammatory TH1 and TH17 cells compared to vehicle treated mice in vivo and following re-stimulation with MOG 35–55 in vitro.
claims.source: Kifunensine treated mice also had more pro-inflammatory TH1 and TH17 cells compared to vehicle treated mice in vivo and following re-stimulation with MOG 35–55 in vitro (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytokine analysis data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The increase in LEA binding began within ~1.5 hr of SW treatment, indicating an almost immediate compensatory response.
claims.source: Although the increase in LEA binding trailed slightly behind an increase in ConA binding, it began to increase within ~1.5 hr of SW treatment, indicating an almost immediate compensatory response.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time course data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Blocking TCR signaling genetically or pharmacologically only partially reduced the magnitude of the poly-LacNAc response induced by SW.
claims.source: Blocking TCR signaling genetically, with TCRβ and Lck deficient Jurkat lines, or pharmacologically, with MAP kinase inhibitors, only partially reduced the magnitude of the poly-LacNAc response induced by SW (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Directly activating downstream TCR signaling with PMA and ionomycin did not induce poly-LacNAc up-regulation, although it further enhanced poly-LacNAc triggered by SW.
claims.source: More importantly, directly activating downstream TCR signaling with PMA and ionomycin did not induce poly-LacNAc up-regulation, although it further enhanced poly-LacNAc triggered by SW (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: TCR signaling appears to be neither necessary nor sufficient for the homeostatic poly-LacNAc response, but does contribute to its magnitude in the context of deficient branching.
claims.source: Thus, TCR signaling appears to be neither necessary nor sufficient for the homeostatic poly-LacNAc response, but does contribute to its magnitude in the context of deficient branching.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data with TCR signaling manipulations.

claims.claim: Microarray analysis of purified Mgat2+/+ and Mgat2-/- CD4+ T cells revealed no significant changes in glycosylation genes known to impact poly-LacNAc production or UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis.
claims.source: Microarray analysis of purified Mgat2+/+ and Mgat2-/- CD4+ T cells revealed no significant changes in glycosylation genes known to impact poly-LacNAc production or UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data presented in Table 1.

claims.claim: Comparing B3GNT2 protein levels in Jurkat T cells treated with or without SW showed no difference.
claims.source: Comparing B3GNT2 protein levels in Jurkat T cells treated with or without SW also showed no difference (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Total poly-LacNAc enzyme activity in lysates from control and SW treated Jurkat T cells revealed no difference.
claims.source: Total poly-LacNAc enzyme activity in lysates from control and SW treated Jurkat T cells also revealed no difference (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Increased B3GNT enzyme activity is not responsible for the homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc induced by branching deficiency.
claims.source: Thus, increased B3GNT enzyme activity is not responsible for the homeostatic up-regulation of poly-LacNAc induced by branching deficiency.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the enzyme activity and protein level data.

claims.claim: All three UDP-GlcNAc transporters localized to the cis and medial Golgi compartments while B3GNT2 localized to a later Golgi compartment.
claims.source: All three UDP-GlcNAc transporters localized to the cis and medial Golgi compartments while B3GNT2 localized to a later Golgi compartment (Figure 5A–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy and line scan analysis data in Figures 5A-E.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the UDP-GlcNAc transporters did not drive poly-LacNAc production.
claims.source: In addition, overexpression of the UDP-GlcNAc transporters did not drive poly-LacNAc production (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The trans Golgi is comparatively deficient in UDP-GlcNAc, thereby limiting B3GNT activity and poly-LacNAc extension under steady state conditions.
claims.source: These results suggest that the trans Golgi is comparatively deficient in UDP-GlcNAc, thereby limiting B3GNT activity and poly-LacNAc extension under steady state conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data and overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: SW treatment did not alter the Golgi localization of the three UDP-GlcNAc transporters or B3GNT2.
claims.source: However, SW treatment did not alter the Golgi localization of the three UDP-GlcNAc transporters or B3GNT2, arguing against this possibility (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by localization data comparing control and SW treated cells in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Measuring UDP-GlcNAc by LC-MS/MS in a whole cell vesicular fraction isolated from post nuclear supernatant revealed significant levels of UDP-GlcNAc.
claims.source: Measuring UDP-GlcNAc by LC-MS/MS in a whole cell vesicular fraction isolated from post nuclear supernatant revealed significant levels of UDP-GlcNAc (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in the referenced figure supplement.

claims.claim: Treatment of post nuclear supernatant with 0.1% Triton-X or 50 mM UMP significantly reduced the amount of UDP-GlcNAc in the vesicular fraction, confirming UDP-GlcNAc was located in vesicles containing UDP-GlcNAc/UMP anti-porters.
claims.source: Both treatments significantly reduced the amount of UDP-GlcNAc in the vesicular fraction, confirming UDP-GlcNAc was located in vesicles containing UDP-GlcNAc/UMP anti-porters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claims.claim: UDP-GlcNAc levels were elevated in the vesicular but not the cytosolic fractions of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells.
claims.source: Consistent with our hypothesis, UDP-GlcNAc levels were elevated in the vesicular but not the cytosolic fractions of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: UDP-GlcNAc was elevated in the Golgi of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells despite no difference in total cellular or cytosolic UDP-GlcNAc levels.
claims.source: UDP-GlcNAc was elevated in the Golgi of kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells despite no difference in total cellular or cytosolic UDP-GlcNAc levels (Figures 4G,6A,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: TGN46 immuno-isolated vesicles from Brefeldin A treated Jurkat T cells were partially depleted for cis and medial Golgi markers relative to trans Golgi markers including B3GNT2, confirming relative enrichment of the trans/TGN compartment.
claims.source: TGN46 immuno-isolated vesicles from Brefeldin A treated Jurkat T cells were partially depleted for cis and medial Golgi markers relative to trans Golgi markers including B3GNT2, confirming relative enrichment of the trans/TGN compartment (Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figures 6D and E.

claims.claim: Vesicles from kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells demonstrated increased UDP-GlcNAc relative to control, indicating that UDP-GlcNAc levels rise in the trans Golgi when medial Golgi branching activity is significantly diminished.
claims.source: Vesicles from kifunensine treated Jurkat T cells demonstrated increased UDP-GlcNAc relative to control (Figure 6F), indicating that UDP-GlcNAc levels rise in the trans Golgi when medial Golgi branching activity is significantly diminished.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Nocodazole, which interrupts longitudinal but not vertical Golgi tubules, had no effect on poly-LacNAc induction by SW in Jurkat T cells.
claims.source: Nocodazole, which interrupts longitudinal but not vertical Golgi tubules, had no effect on poly-LacNAc induction by SW in Jurkat T cells (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Pyrrophenone significantly blocked SW induced up-regulation of poly-LacNAc in Jurkat T cells in a dose dependent manner.
claims.source: In contrast, pyrrophenone disrupts both longitudinal and inter-cisternal vertical tubules via inhibition of cytosolic phospholipase A2-α (San Pietro et al., 2009). Pyrrophenone significantly blocked SW induced up-regulation of poly-LacNAc in Jurkat T cells in a dose dependent manner, as indicated by comparing its effects on LEA and ConA staining; the latter controlling for any changes in Golgi transport (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Pyrrophenone had no effect on ConA, LEA, or L-PHA levels in control Jurkat T cells lacking SW.
claims.source: In contrast, pyrrophenone had no effect on ConA, LEA, or L-PHA levels in control Jurkat T cells lacking SW (Figure 6—supplement figure 1F–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the referenced figure supplement.

claims.claim: When branching enzymes under-utilize UDP-GlcNAc in the medial Golgi, UDP-GlcNAc accumulates and then shifts by diffusion to the trans Golgi via inter-cisternal tubules, thereby increasing substrate supply to B3GNT and triggering poly-LacNAc extension.
claims.source: We conclude that when branching enzymes under-utilize UDP-GlcNAc in the medial Golgi, UDP-GlcNAc accumulates and then shifts by diffusion to the trans Golgi via inter-cisternal tubules, thereby increasing substrate supply to B3GNT and triggering poly-LacNAc extension (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by the UDP-GlcNAc measurements and pyrrophenone inhibition data.

claims.claim: Structurally disparate glycans are functionally equivalent based on LacNAc content.
claims.source: Our data demonstrates that structurally disparate glycans are functionally equivalent based on LacNAc content and suggests a novel self-correcting mechanism in the Golgi that sustains cellular homeostasis by ensuring LacNAc content is maintained at a minimal level within N-glycans.
claims.evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study based on the functional equivalence of Mgat2 and Mgat5 deficient T cells.

claims.claim: The Golgi has a novel self-correcting mechanism that sustains cellular homeostasis by ensuring LacNAc content is maintained at a minimal level within N-glycans.
claims.source: Our data demonstrates that structurally disparate glycans are functionally equivalent based on LacNAc content and suggests a novel self-correcting mechanism in the Golgi that sustains cellular homeostasis by ensuring LacNAc content is maintained at a minimal level within N-glycans.
claims.evidence: This is the main conceptual conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: The similar degree of hyperactivity between Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient T cells indicates that poly-LacNAc extended hybrid structures are functionally equivalent to complex tri-antennary structures.
claims.source: The similar degree of hyperactivity between Mgat5 and Mgat2 deficient T cells indicates that poly-LacNAc extended hybrid structures are functionally equivalent to complex tri-antennary structures.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data comparing the two genotypes.

claims.claim: Blockade of mannosidase II and Mgat2 deficiency produced a similar phenotype, which was blocked/reversed by both mannosidase I inhibition and Mgat1 deficiency, despite each targeting distinct biochemical steps and resulting in distinct structures.
claims.source: Importantly, blockade of mannosidase II and Mgat2 deficiency produced a similar phenotype, which was blocked/reversed by both mannosidase I inhibition and Mgat1 deficiency, despite each targeting distinct biochemical steps and resulting in distinct structures.
claims.evidence: This is based on the experimental data with different inhibitors and genetic models.

claims.claim: Structurally diverse glycans are biologically equivalent if they share a similar amount of LacNAc.
claims.source: Thus, our data demonstrate that structurally diverse glycans are biologically equivalent if they share a similar amount of LacNAc.
claims.evidence: This is a key conclusion based on the functional equivalence data.

claims.claim: The overall glycan structure sets the total LacNAc content, thereby largely determining avidity of binding for galectins.
claims.source: The overall glycan structure sets the total LacNAc content, thereby largely determining avidity of binding for galectins.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the data and understanding of multivalent binding.

claims.claim: Glycan diversity may be collapsed into a much smaller group of bioequivalent structures based on the number of structural subunits within the overall glycan that bind to a given animal lectin.
claims.source: Our data suggests that glycan diversity may be collapsed into a much smaller group of bioequivalent structures based on the number of structural subunits within the overall glycan that bind to a given animal lectin.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual inference based on the findings of functional equivalence.

claims.claim: N-glycosylation is an essential biosynthetic pathway necessary for cellular homeostasis and mammalian development.
claims.source: N-glycosylation is an essential biosynthetic pathway necessary for cellular homeostasis and mammalian development (Dennis et al., 2009), yet lacks a known self-correcting mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Homeostatic control of LacNAc content does not result from changes in enzyme levels/activity or metabolic production of UDP-GlcNAc substrate.
claims.source: Our data suggest that homeostatic control of LacNAc content does not result from changes in enzyme levels/activity or metabolic production of UDP-GlcNAc substrate; but rather appears to arise from the structure of the Golgi.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microarray, Western blot, enzyme activity, and UDP-GlcNAc measurement data.

claims.claim: The UDP-GlcNAc transporters preferentially supply UDP-GlcNAc to the cis/medial over trans Golgi, thus prioritizing branching over extension.
claims.source: Our data indicate that the UDP-GlcNAc transporters preferentially supply UDP-GlcNAc to the cis/medial over trans Golgi, thus prioritizing branching over extension.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization data and functional studies.

claims.claim: The segmented organization of enzymes and transporters allows for local depletion of substrate prior to diffusion to other compartments.
claims.source: Despite the presence of continuities between Golgi cisterna and previous work arguing that the Golgi is functionally interconnected (Kim et al., 2001), our data suggest that the segmented organization of enzymes and transporters allows for local depletion of substrate prior to diffusion to other compartments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and UDP-GlcNAc distribution data.

claims.claim: The evolutionary placement of the B3GNT poly-LacNAc extension enzymes in the trans Golgi provides a backup mechanism that captures unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi shunted via inter-cisternal tubules.
claims.source: In this manner, the evolutionary placement of the B3GNT poly-LacNAc extension enzymes in the trans Golgi provides a backup mechanism that captures unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi shunted via inter-cisternal tubules.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual inference about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claims.claim: This backup system may explain the lack of evolutionary pressure to produce genetic redundancy in the Golgi branching enzymes in mammals.
claims.source: This backup system may also explain the lack of evolutionary pressure to produce genetic redundancy in the Golgi branching enzymes in mammals and the dramatically more severe phenotype seen with Mgat1 deficiency, which blocks all production of N-glycan LacNAc, compared to other Mgat genes (Ioffe and Stanley, 1994; Metzler et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary implications.

claims.claim: High protein transit rates present a significant challenge to the Golgi and have the potential to reduce the medial Golgi branching efficiency by decreasing the time available for branching reactions.
claims.source: High protein transit rates present a significant challenge to the Golgi and have the potential to reduce the medial Golgi branching efficiency by decreasing the time available for branching reactions.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential physiological challenges.

claims.claim: Having a back-up system that provides poly-LacNAc extension in the trans Golgi by capturing unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi would be critical for the maintenance of the lattice at a minimal essential level.
claims.source: Under this scenario, having a back-up system that provides poly-LacNAc extension in the trans Golgi by capturing unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial Golgi would be critical for the maintenance of the lattice at a minimal essential level.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of the mechanism.

claims.claim: A second step in the assembly line would act to counteract the moment to moment variability and stochastic uncertainty of glycan synthesis.
claims.source: Even in an unstressed system, a second step in the assembly line would act to counteract the moment to moment variability and stochastic uncertainty of glycan synthesis.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the general function of the mechanism.

claims.claim: The effectiveness of SW as an anti-cancer therapeutic is likely limited by compensatory poly-LacNAc production.
claims.source: For example, the effectiveness of SW as an anti-cancer therapeutic is likely limited by compensatory poly-LacNAc production (Goss et al., 1994; 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference about therapeutic implications based on the findings.

claims.claim: Therapeutic strategies aimed at disrupting the lattice should block branching and extension simultaneously, or target a more proximal regulator such as UDP-GlcNAc metabolism or transport.
claims.source: Thus, therapeutic strategies aimed at disrupting the lattice should block branching and extension simultaneously, or target a more proximal regulator such as UDP-GlcNAc metabolism or transport.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: Increased availability and use of UDP-GlcNAc in the trans Golgi would increase uridine-monophosphate (UMP) levels, thereby driving anti-port of UDP-Galactose into the trans Golgi to promote further extension with poly-LacNAc rather than capping by sialic acid.
claims.source: Increased availability and use of UDP-GlcNAc in the trans Golgi would increase uridine-monophosphate (UMP) levels, thereby driving anti-port of UDP-Galactose into the trans Golgi to promote further extension with poly-LacNAc rather than capping by sialic acid.

claims.claim: B3GNT2 is one of the major B3GNT enzymes responsible for poly-LacNAc branch extension in mouse T cells.
claims.source: B3GNT2 is one of the major B3GNT enzymes responsible for poly-LacNAc branch extension in mouse T cells and poly-LacNAc up-regulation is expected to be limited in its absence (Togayachi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

results.result: The Golgi apparatus has a self-correcting mechanism that maintains cellular homeostasis by generating bioequivalent N-glycans when branching is deficient. Mgat2 and Mgat5 deficient T cells show similar activation levels despite different degrees of branching deficiency, with poly-LacNAc extension compensating for reduced branching to maintain comparable galectin-3 binding and LacNAc content.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C31 provide direct experimental evidence showing similar T cell activation and galectin-3 binding between Mgat2 and Mgat5 deficient cells despite different branching levels. Claims C35, C46, C47 demonstrate increased poly-LacNAc in Mgat2 deficient cells. The functional equivalence is supported by multiple experimental approaches including flow cytometry, mass spectrometry, and functional assays. This represents the core finding of the manuscript.

results.result: Poly-LacNAc extension is triggered by redistribution of unused UDP-GlcNAc from the medial to trans-Golgi via inter-cisternal tubules. UDP-GlcNAc transporters localize to cis/medial Golgi while B3GNT2 localizes to trans Golgi, and UDP-GlcNAc levels increase in trans Golgi compartments when branching is inhibited.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C71, C72, C74 provide direct experimental evidence from confocal microscopy localization studies and mass spectrometry measurements of UDP-GlcNAc in different Golgi compartments. Claim C76 shows pyrrophenone (which disrupts inter-cisternal tubules) blocks poly-LacNAc induction in a dose-dependent manner, while C75 shows nocodazole (which only disrupts longitudinal tubules) has no effect. This mechanistic model is well-supported by converging lines of evidence.

results.result: Homeostatic poly-LacNAc extension functionally opposes T cell hyperactivity and autoimmunity. Blocking poly-LacNAc extension (genetically or pharmacologically) in branching-deficient T cells increases T cell activation, proliferation, and severity of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 provide consistent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (pharmacological inhibition with kifunensine/DMN and genetic deletion of B3gnt2) showing increased T cell hyperactivity when poly-LacNAc is blocked. Claims C54-C56 demonstrate in vivo functional consequences in the EAE model with increased disease severity and pro-inflammatory cytokines. The dose-response relationship (C51) strengthens the causal interpretation.

results.result: Inhibition of N-glycan branching results in compensatory poly-LacNAc extension on N-glycans. Mgat2 deficiency causes ~100-fold increase in LEA binding (poly-LacNAc marker), which is blocked by Mgat1 deficiency and mannosidase I inhibitors, and confirmed by mass spectrometry showing hybrid N-glycans with extended poly-LacNAc chains.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C43-C45 provide converging evidence that poly-LacNAc induction requires MGAT1 activity and is specific to the N-glycan pathway. Claim C41 shows >80% reduction in LEA binding with PNGase F treatment, confirming N-glycan localization. Claims C46-C47 provide direct structural evidence from MALDI-TOF-MS and endo-β-galactosidase digestion showing increased poly-LacNAc chain length. The response is general across cell types (C37).

results.result: Homeostatic poly-LacNAc up-regulation does not result from increased B3GNT enzyme activity or transcriptional changes. TCR signaling is neither necessary nor sufficient for the response, and no changes in B3GNT2 protein levels, enzyme activity, or glycosylation gene expression were detected.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 provide direct negative evidence from microarray, Western blot, and enzyme activity assays showing no changes in B3GNT expression or activity. Claims C58-C60 demonstrate through genetic and pharmacological manipulation that TCR signaling contributes to but is not required for the response. This effectively rules out transcriptional/translational mechanisms and narrows the mechanism to substrate availability.

results.result: UDP-GlcNAc levels increase specifically in Golgi vesicular fractions when branching is inhibited, without changes in total cellular or cytosolic UDP-GlcNAc. Trans-Golgi enriched fractions show elevated UDP-GlcNAc in kifunensine-treated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 establish the methodology for measuring vesicular UDP-GlcNAc with appropriate controls (Triton-X and UMP treatment). Claims C71-C72 show selective elevation in vesicular but not cytosolic fractions. Claims C73-C74 demonstrate increased UDP-GlcNAc specifically in trans-Golgi enriched fractions using Brefeldin A treatment and TGN46 immunoisolation. The compartment-specific changes support the redistribution model.

results.result: Pyrrophenone, which disrupts inter-cisternal Golgi tubules, blocks swainsonine-induced poly-LacNAc up-regulation in a dose-dependent manner, while nocodazole (which only disrupts longitudinal tubules) has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 shows dose-dependent inhibition of poly-LacNAc induction by pyrrophenone with appropriate controls (ConA staining to control for general Golgi transport effects). Claim C75 provides negative control showing nocodazole has no effect. Claim C77 shows pyrrophenone has no effect in the absence of swainsonine, indicating specificity for the compensatory response. This pharmacological evidence strongly supports the inter-cisternal tubule redistribution mechanism.

results.result: Mgat5 deficiency reduces galectin-3 binding and causes T-cell hyperactivity and autoimmunity, as previously established.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C22 cite previous work establishing this phenotype. Claim C30 provides confirmatory data in the current study showing reduced galectin-3 binding in Mgat5-/- T cells. This represents established prior knowledge that provides context for the current findings.

results.result: Mgat2 deficiency is expected to have a more severe impact on N-glycan branching than Mgat5 deficiency based on the sequential nature of the pathway and enzyme kinetics. T cell-specific Mgat2 deletion was confirmed by loss of L-PHA binding in most T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are based on established knowledge of the biosynthetic pathway and enzyme kinetics (cited). Claim C27 provides experimental confirmation of Mgat2 deletion in the mouse model using L-PHA staining. Claim C28 establishes the specificity of L-PHA for β1,6GlcNAc branches. This provides essential characterization of the genetic model.

results.result: LEA lectin binds to poly-LacNAc structures containing at least three repeating LacNAc units. Wild type and Mgat5-/- T cells express very low levels of poly-LacNAc. Poly-LacNAc can occur on multiple glycan types, and LEA may also bind high-mannose structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C38, C39 cite established knowledge about LEA specificity. Claim C34 provides baseline data showing low poly-LacNAc in control cells. These claims establish the methodological basis for using LEA as a poly-LacNAc marker, though C39 raises a potential specificity concern that is addressed by subsequent experiments (C40-C45).

results.result: The increased LEA staining in Mgat2 deficient cells is primarily due to poly-LacNAc on N-glycans rather than O-glycans or glycolipids, as demonstrated by PNGase F treatment and comparison with Mgat1 deficient cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 show that PNGase F treatment reduces LEA binding by >80% despite only partially removing N-glycans, indicating N-glycan localization. Claims C42-C45 provide genetic and pharmacological evidence that the response requires MGAT1 activity and is blocked by mannosidase I inhibitors. This addresses the potential specificity concern raised by C39 and confirms N-glycan localization.

results.result: The increase in LEA binding begins within ~1.5 hours of swainsonine treatment, indicating a rapid compensatory response.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by time course data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The rapid kinetics argue against transcriptional mechanisms and support a substrate-driven mechanism. However, the claim notes LEA increase trails slightly behind ConA increase, which is consistent with the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The galectin-glycoprotein lattice is formed by multivalent interactions between galectins and LacNAc units on N-glycans, which are generated by sequential action of Golgi enzymes. The lattice regulates cell surface receptor dynamics and is implicated in various diseases.
results.evaluation: These claims (C7-C18) represent established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to previous work. They provide essential context for understanding the significance of the current findings. The claims are well-established in the field and appropriately cited.

results.result: Previous studies have observed unusual glycan structures in glycosylation pathway deficient mice, leading to speculation about bioequivalent glycan production, but direct evidence was lacking prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 accurately characterize the state of prior knowledge and identify the gap that the current study addresses. The citations support the claims about previous observations and speculation. This establishes the novelty and significance of the current work.

results.result: The existing model predicted that more severe branching deficiency should cause greater T cell hyperactivity, but experimental results revealed the Golgi has capacity to buffer such challenges.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 represents a logical prediction from the existing model. Claim C24 states the surprising finding that contradicts this prediction, which is supported by the experimental data (C29, C31). This framing effectively highlights the novelty of the findings.

results.result: The authors hypothesized that compensatory LacNAc maintenance in Mgat2 deficient T cells would occur through poly-LacNAc extension of the MGAT1-generated branch.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 represents a reasonable hypothesis based on knowledge of the sequential biosynthetic pathway. This hypothesis is then tested and confirmed by subsequent experiments (C35-C47). The claim appropriately distinguishes hypothesis from experimental result.

results.result: Blockade of mannosidase II and Mgat2 deficiency produced similar phenotypes that were reversed by mannosidase I inhibition and Mgat1 deficiency, despite targeting distinct biochemical steps.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 synthesizes results from multiple experiments (C43-C45, C29) showing that different interventions affecting the same pathway step produce similar outcomes. This supports the functional equivalence concept and demonstrates the robustness of the findings across different experimental approaches.

results.result: The overall glycan structure determines total LacNAc content and thus galectin binding avidity. Glycan diversity may be collapsed into bioequivalent structures based on binding subunits for animal lectins.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is a reasonable inference from the data showing functional equivalence based on LacNAc content. However, Claim C85 is more speculative, extrapolating beyond the current data to propose a general principle. While the concept is supported by the current findings, broader validation across different lectins and glycan types would be needed to fully support this generalization.

results.result: N-glycosylation is essential for cellular homeostasis but lacked a known self-correcting mechanism. Homeostatic control of LacNAc content does not result from changes in enzyme levels/activity or UDP-GlcNAc metabolism but appears to arise from Golgi structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 is established knowledge (cited). Claim C87 is supported by negative results from multiple approaches (C61-C64, C71-C72) ruling out transcriptional, translational, and metabolic mechanisms. The conclusion that the mechanism arises from Golgi structure is supported by the localization and compartmentalization data (C65-C78).

results.result: The evolutionary placement of B3GNT enzymes in the trans Golgi provides a backup mechanism for maintaining the galectin-glycoprotein lattice. This may explain the lack of genetic redundancy in mammalian branching enzymes and the severe phenotype of Mgat1 deficiency.
results.evaluation: These claims (C90-C94) represent speculative inferences about evolutionary and physiological significance. While the proposed backup mechanism is supported by the experimental data, the evolutionary explanations (C90-C91) and physiological scenarios (C92-C94) are plausible but not directly tested. These represent reasonable speculation based on the findings but would require additional evidence to fully support.

results.result: The effectiveness of swainsonine as an anti-cancer therapeutic may be limited by compensatory poly-LacNAc production. Therapeutic strategies should target branching and extension simultaneously or target UDP-GlcNAc metabolism/transport.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is a reasonable inference from the findings, supported by citation to previous SW therapeutic trials. However, the therapeutic recommendations in C96 are speculative and not directly tested in the current study. While the logic is sound based on the mechanism, actual therapeutic efficacy would need to be demonstrated experimentally.

results.result: Increased UDP-GlcNAc usage in the trans Golgi would increase UMP levels, driving UDP-Galactose import to promote poly-LacNAc extension rather than sialic acid capping. The use of different nucleotides for different sugars may coordinate these processes.
results.evaluation: These claims (C97-C98) represent mechanistic speculation about how the antiport system coordinates extension versus capping. While the logic is biochemically sound and consistent with the findings, these specific predictions about UMP/UDP-Galactose dynamics and the evolutionary rationale for different nucleotides are not directly tested. Additional experiments measuring these metabolites and their effects would be needed.

results.result: B3GNT2 is one of the major B3GNT enzymes responsible for poly-LacNAc extension in mouse T cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is supported by citation to previous work (Togayachi et al., 2007) and is confirmed functionally in the current study by the B3gnt2 knockout experiments (C52-C53) showing reduced galectin-3 binding and increased T cell hyperactivity when B3gnt2 is deleted.
